title: atlas.json — how one repository describes itself to the Atlas
description: Every repository on the Atlas keeps one atlas.json at its root. It says what the repository is, where it is up to, what it is made of, what it offers other repositories and what it takes from them. The Atlas (cdomotor-g/atlas) reads every one of these files every few hours and draws the map from them. Links are declared by the CONSUMER, in `consumes`, because the consumer is the one that breaks when the provider changes. The file is public: no landholder details, site codes, secrets or private issue text.

id.description: This repository's id on the Atlas — the key in the Atlas's data/registry.json.

name.description: The name a person reads (Flood-Net, not MegaNet).

about.description: Two to four plain sentences: what it does and who it is for.

kind.description: A few words: web app, firmware, base-station OS, static site, content pipeline…

logo.description: Path to a logo or picture in this repository (svg, png, jpg or webp). The Atlas keeps its own copy in assets/logos/ and uses that first.

docs.description: Paths in this repository: readme, roadmap, agents (CLAUDE.md) and anything else worth a link.

version.description: Where the current version is written down, so the Atlas can show it.

pattern.description: A regular expression whose first group is the version.

releases.description: true when the version is published as GitHub releases.

updated.description: The date this status was last checked against the repository.

summary.description: One sentence: where it is up to, today.

now.description: What is being worked on. #123 links to an issue here; owner/repo#123 to one elsewhere.

next.description: What comes after, roughly in order.

what.description: What is blocked, in a line. #123 links an issue here.

on.description: Who or what it waits on: "human" (only the owner can clear it: hardware, money or a judgment call), "computer" (an agent at the owner's computer can clear it signed in as them — a dashboard, a setting, an account page, a repository to create; the owner approves and types any password), "agent" (an agent could clear it from anywhere, nobody has yet), another Atlas id, or an issue as id#123. Before writing "human", ask whether all it needs is the owner's sign-in: then it is "computer". The Atlas shows a "human" blocker of kind access with "computer" too.

id.description: A short id, so another repository's `holds` or a later note can point at it. Until the blocker has an issue, the Atlas shows it by this id (its tag, and the end of its address: #blockers/<repo>/<id>), so give every blocker one.

kind.description: decision: someone has to choose. access: an account, a secret or a setting behind the owner's sign-in — an agent at their computer can do it signed in as them, so it goes on "computer". hardware: needs a device, a site or a bench. money: needs spending. upstream: waits on another repository or vendor. time: waits for data to accumulate or a date.

issue.description: The issue that tracks it: #123 here, or owner/repo#123.

holds.description: What it holds up: issue refs (#123, owner/repo#123), Atlas ids of other repositories, or short phrases. The Atlas ranks blockers by how much they hold.

options.description: The ways through it that you can see — including partial ones and workarounds. Mark the one you would pick with recommended: true.

what.description: The step, concretely enough to start on.

by.description: Who can do it: "human" (the owner, by hand), "computer" (an agent at the owner's computer, signed in as them: Claude in Chrome for websites, computer use for desktop apps, Claude Code in a folder shared through Remote Control), "agent" (any session, from anywhere), or another Atlas id.

effort.description: Rough size: "10 min", "an afternoon", or Low / Med / High.

model.description: For an agent: the recommended model and effort, as in issue titles (Sonnet5/Med).

issue.description: An issue for this option, if one exists.

blocked.description: What is stopping work, what it holds up, and the ways through it. The Atlas draws each one on the map (to you, to your computer, to an agent, or to the repository it waits on) and lists them in its Blockers view, most-holding first.

components.description: The parts worth seeing on the map when you zoom in. Five to twelve is about right.

provides.description: What other repositories may rely on: a file, a format, an API, a build. Changing one of these is what the Atlas's forward propagation is about.

component.description: The component above it belongs to.

contract.description: Path to the document that defines it.

consumes.description: Everything this repository takes from another. Each entry becomes a line on the map.

provider.description: Which of the provider's `provides` (or components) this is.

into.description: Which of this repository's components takes it.

how.description: vendored: a verbatim copy kept here. generated: data made here from the provider's. built: the provider's source built into something here. live: read at run time. release: reads the provider's latest release. protocol: implements a format or protocol the provider defines. reference: links to or cites it. ported: taken from it once, now independent.

url.description: For live links: what is read.

watch.description: Paths in the provider whose change matters here. A trailing / means everything under it; * matches within a name.

since.description: The point this repository last caught up with the provider. Upstream commits to `watch` after it are drift.

file.description: A file in THIS repository that records the provider commit.

pattern.description: Regular expression; first group is the commit.

on_change.description: What to do here when the provider changes what is watched.

drift_issue.description: true: the drift check opens an issue in this repository when the provider has moved on. Default false (the Atlas shows it either way).

asks.description: Back propagation: things this repository needs another to change. File them as issues in the other repository when you can and put the issue here; until then the Atlas shows the ask on the line between the two.
